newsitem.title: CHINA: China plans to expand national cotton market.
newsitem.headline: China plans to expand national cotton market.

text.p: China plans to set up nationwide spot and futures cotton markets by gradually expanding trade fairs to replace existing state controls, but officials said on Monday the reform faces difficulties.
China last week held its second national cotton trade fair, in Beijing, with 85 state cotton and flax firms and more than 100 textile firms taking part.

Total contracts signed reached 320,000 tonnes, with value at about 6.0 billion yuan ($72 million), a senior official of the Cotton and Flax Bureau of the All-China Association of Supply and Marketing Cooperatives said in a telephone interview.

Officials of the association that oversees state purchases, allocation and trading declared the fair a success even though only about 40 percent of total contracts signed were expected to result in actual deals.
Nearly half of the cotton was bought by the China National Cotton Corp, a unit of the association and the main state cotton company handling state reserves, imports and exports.
"We bought the cotton mainly for reserves," a company official said.
However, the second fair was far larger than the first, held last November in the central city of Zhengzhou, when a mere nine cotton firms turned up, the association official said.
This time it was opened to state cotton and flax firms at county levels in addition to national-level firms.
Textile firms involved increased by 10 percent.
"The purpose of holding such trade fairs is gradually to establish China's cotton marketing system to replace the current state planning," the official said.
"Although the fairs are still at an initial stage, this is an essential step for the development of a large-scale spot and futures cotton market."
China expected to establish a national cotton trading system in the next two to three years, he said.
But the development of such a market would go hand-in-hand with measures to protect cotton farmers from excessive price fluctuations, he said.
"It needs about two to three years," he said.
China's cotton resources are now largely controlled by the state, with only state firms allowed to buy from farmers and supply the textile industry in line with government-set quotas.
China still bans cotton trading outside the trade fairs.

But recent tight market conditions had forced many ailing textile enterprises to import cheap foreign cotton or to buy secretly from cotton firms at prices lower than the high official quota prices, officials said.
"We bought little cotton at the fair," said an official of the Beijing No 2 Textile Factory, even though prices at the fair were about one to two percent lower than state prices.
The factory obtained cheaper cotton from cash-strapped state cotton firms eager to cut stockpiles, she said.
"Currently, supply has exceeded demand," the official of the Cotton and Flax Bureau said. "This is unlikely to change in the short term."
